content: The definition of multivessel disease for inclusion in the AEGIS-II study is as follows: 1. Index Myocardial Infarction (MI) Cardiac Catheterization Findings: Multivessel disease can be identified if there is evidence of 50% or greater stenosis in the left main coronary artery or in at least two of the major coronary artery territories (left anterior descending [LAD], left circumflex [LCx], or right coronary artery [RCA]) prior to any interventions being performed. 2. Prior Cardiac Catheterization Findings: Multivessel disease can also be identified if a prior cardiac catheterization demonstrates 50% or greater stenosis in the left main coronary artery or in at least two of the major coronary artery territories (LAD, LCx, or RCA) prior to any interventions being performed. 3. Combination of Index MI and Prior Percutaneous Coronary Intervention (PCI): Multivessel disease can be diagnosed if the index MI cardiac catheterization shows 50% or greater stenosis in one vessel (prior to any interventions) and there is evidence of prior PCI involving at least one vessel that is different from the vessel associated with the index MI. 4. Prior Multivessel Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting (CABG): Multivessel disease can also be defined by a history of multivessel CABG. 5. General Criteria for Multivessel Disease: Multivessel disease requires the presence of 50% or greater stenosis in at least two of the three major epicardial coronary artery territories (LAD, LCx, or RCA) or in the left main coronary artery. Disease in branch vessels may qualify as part of the territory of the corresponding major vessel. For example, a diagonal branch is considered part of the LAD territory. 6. Special Considerations for Vessel Territories: For the purposes of this study, the ramus intermedius is considered part of the left circumflex artery (LCx) territory. Additionally, vessels must have a diameter of greater than 2 mm to be included in the assessment.
